                [0-703] paragraph
                  [0-704] StaticText: For decades the recommended style was to break after binary operators. But this can hurt readability in two ways: the operators tend to get scattered across different columns on the screen, and each operator is moved away from its operand and onto the previous line.                   [0-741] StaticText: To solve this readability problem, mathematicians and their publishers follow the opposite convention. Donald Knuth explains the traditional rule in his

                  [0-748] StaticText: Following the tradition from mathematics usually results in more readable code:

              [0-786] section
                [0-787] heading: Blank Lines
                  [0-788] doc-backlink: Blank Lines
                [0-790] paragraph
                  [0-791] StaticText: Surround top-level function and class definitions with two blank lines.
                [0-792] paragraph
                  [0-793] StaticText: Method definitions inside a class are surrounded by a single blank line.
                [0-794] paragraph
                  [0-795] StaticText: Extra blank lines may be used (sparingly) to separate groups of related functions. Blank lines may be omitted between a bunch of related one-liners (e.g. a set of dummy implementations).
                [0-796] paragraph
                  [0-797] StaticText: Use blank lines in functions, sparingly, to indicate logical sections.
                [0-798] paragraph
                  [0-799] StaticText: Python accepts the control-L (i.e. ^L) form feed character as whitespace; many tools treat these characters as page separators, so you may use them to separate pages of related sections of your file. Note, some editors and web-based code viewers may not recognize control-L as a form feed and will show another glyph in its place.
              [0-800] section
                [0-801] heading: Source File Encoding
                  [0-802] doc-backlink: Source File Encoding
                [0-804] paragraph
                  [0-805] StaticText: Code in the core Python distribution should always use UTF-8, and should not have an encoding declaration.
                [0-806] paragraph
                  [0-807] StaticText: In the standard library, non-UTF-8 encodings should be used only for test purposes. Use non-ASCII characters sparingly, preferably only to denote places and human names. If using non-ASCII characters as data, avoid noisy Unicode characters like z̯̯͡a̧͎̺l̡͓̫g̹̲o̡̼̘ and byte order marks.
                [0-808] paragraph
                  [0-809] StaticText: All identifiers in the Python standard library MUST use ASCII-only identifiers, and SHOULD use English words wherever feasible (in many cases, abbreviations and technical terms are used which aren’t English).
                [0-810] paragraph
                  [0-811] StaticText: Open source projects with a global audience are encouraged to adopt a similar policy.

                  [0-869] listitem
                    [0-4067] ListMarker: •

                    [0-1470] StaticText: Avoid trailing whitespace anywhere. Because it’s usually invisible, it can be confusing: e.g. a backslash followed by a space and a newline does not count as a line continuation marker. Some editors don’t preserve it and many projects (like CPython itself) have pre-commit hooks that reject it.

            [0-2032] section
              [0-2033] heading: When to Use Trailing Commas
                [0-2034] doc-backlink: When to Use Trailing Commas
              [0-2036] paragraph
                [0-2037] StaticText: Trailing commas are usually optional, except they are mandatory when making a tuple of one element. For clarity, it is recommended to surround the latter in (technically redundant) parentheses:
              [0-2038] pre
                [0-2039] StaticText: # Correct:
                [0-2040] StaticText: 
                [0-2041] StaticText: FILES
                [0-2042] StaticText: 
                [0-2043] StaticText: =
                [0-2044] StaticText: 
                [0-2045] StaticText: (
                [0-2046] StaticText: 'setup.cfg'
                [0-2047] StaticText: ,)
                [0-2048] StaticText: 
              [0-2049] pre
                [0-2050] StaticText: # Wrong:
                [0-2051] StaticText: 
                [0-2052] StaticText: FILES
                [0-2053] StaticText: 
                [0-2054] StaticText: =
                [0-2055] StaticText: 
                [0-2056] StaticText: 'setup.cfg'
                [0-2057] StaticText: ,
                [0-2058] StaticText: 
              [0-2059] paragraph
                [0-2060] StaticText: When trailing commas are redundant, they are often helpful when a version control system is used, when a list of values, arguments or imported items is expected to be extended over time. The pattern is to put each value (etc.) on a line by itself, always adding a trailing comma, and add the close parenthesis/bracket/brace on the next line. However it does not make sense to have a trailing comma on the same line as the closing delimiter (except in the above case of singleton tuples):
              [0-2061] pre
                [0-2062] StaticText: # Correct:
                [0-2063] StaticText:

            [0-2114] section
              [0-2115] heading: Comments
                [0-48] doc-backlink: Comments
              [0-2117] paragraph
                [0-2118] StaticText: Comments that contradict the code are worse than no comments. Always make a priority of keeping the comments up-to-date when the code changes!
              [0-2119] paragraph
                [0-2120] StaticText: Comments should be complete sentences. The first word should be capitalized, unless it is an identifier that begins with a lower case letter (never alter the case of identifiers!).
              [0-2121] paragraph
                [0-2122] StaticText: Block comments generally consist of one or more paragraphs built out of complete sentences, with each sentence ending in a period.
              [0-2123] paragraph
                [0-2124] StaticText: You should use one or two spaces after a sentence-ending period in multi-sentence comments, except after the final sentence.
              [0-2125] paragraph
                [0-2126] StaticText: Ensure that your comments are clear and easily understandable to other speakers of the language you are writing in.
              [0-2127] paragraph
                [0-2128] StaticText: Python coders from non-English speaking countries: please write your comments in English, unless you are 120% sure that the code will never be read by people who don’t speak your language.
              [0-2129] section
                [0-2130] heading: Block Comments
                  [0-2131] doc-backlink: Block Comments
                [0-2133] paragraph
                  [0-2134] StaticText: Block comments generally apply to some (or all) code that follows them, and are indented to the same level as that code. Each line of a block comment starts with a
                  [0-4941] code
                    [0-2135] StaticText: #
                  [0-2136] StaticText: and a single space (unless it is indented text inside the comment).
                [0-2137] paragraph
                  [0-2138] StaticText: Paragraphs inside a block comment are separated by a line containing a single
                  [0-4943] code
                    [0-2139] StaticText: #
                  [0-2140] StaticText: .
              [0-2141] section
                [0-2142] heading: Inline Comments
                  [0-2143] doc-backlink: Inline Comments
                [0-2145] paragraph
                  [0-2146] StaticText: Use inline comments sparingly.
                [0-2147] paragraph
                  [0-2148] StaticText: An inline comment is a comment on the same line as a statement. Inline comments should be separated by at least two spaces from the statement. They should start with a # and a single space.
                [0-2149] paragraph
                  [0-2150] StaticText: Inline comments are unnecessary and in fact distracting if they state the obvious. Don’t do this:
                [0-2151] pre
                  [0-2152] StaticText: x

                  [0-2154] StaticText: =

                  [0-2162] StaticText: # Increment x
                  [0-2163] StaticText: 
                [0-2164] paragraph
                  [0-2165] StaticText: But sometimes, this is useful:
                [0-2166] pre

              [0-2179] section
                [0-2180] heading: Documentation Strings
                  [0-2181] doc-backlink: Documentation Strings
                [0-2183] paragraph
                  [0-2184] StaticText: Conventions for writing good documentation strings (a.k.a. “docstrings”) are immortalized in
                  [0-2185] link: PEP 257
                  [0-2187] StaticText: .
                [0-2188] list
                  [0-2189] listitem
                    [0-4963] ListMarker: •
                    [0-2190] StaticText: Write docstrings for all public modules, functions, classes, and methods. Docstrings are not necessary for non-public methods, but you should have a comment that describes what the method does. This comment should appear after the
                    [0-4964] code
                      [0-2191] StaticText: def
                    [0-2192] StaticText: line.
                  [0-2193] listitem
                    [0-4966] ListMarker: •
                    [0-2194] link: PEP 257
                    [0-2196] StaticText: describes good docstring conventions. Note that most importantly, the
                    [0-4967] code
                      [0-2197] StaticText: """
                    [0-2198] StaticText: that ends a multiline docstring should be on a line by itself:
                    [0-2199] pre
                      [0-2200] StaticText: """Return a foobang
                      [0-2201] StaticText: 
                      [0-2202] StaticText: Optional plotz says to frobnicate the bizbaz first.
                      [0-2203] StaticText: 
                      [0-2204] StaticText: """
                      [0-2205] StaticText: 
                  [0-2206] listitem
                    [0-4975] ListMarker: •
                    [0-2207] StaticText: For one liner docstrings, please keep the closing
                    [0-4976] code
                      [0-2208] StaticText: """
                    [0-2209] StaticText: on the same line:
                    [0-2210] pre
                      [0-2211] StaticText: """Return an ex-parrot."""
                      [0-2212] StaticText: 
            [0-2213] section
              [0-2214] heading: Naming Conventions
                [0-2215] doc-backlink: Naming Conventions
              [0-2217] paragraph
                [0-2218] StaticText: The naming conventions of Python’s library are a bit of a mess, so we’ll never get this completely consistent – nevertheless, here are the currently recommended naming standards. New modules and packages (including third party frameworks) should be written to these standards, but where an existing library has a different style, internal consistency is preferred.
              [0-2219] section
                [0-2220] heading: Overriding Principle
                  [0-2221] doc-backlink: Overriding Principle
                [0-2223] paragraph
                  [0-2224] StaticText: Names that are visible to the user as public parts of the API should follow conventions that reflect usage rather than implementation.
              [0-2225] section
                [0-2226] heading: Descriptive: Naming Styles
                  [0-2227] doc-backlink: Descriptive: Naming Styles
                [0-2229] paragraph
                  [0-2230] StaticText: There are a lot of different naming styles. It helps to be able to recognize what naming style is being used, independently from what they are used for.
                [0-2231] paragraph
                  [0-2232] StaticText: The following naming styles are commonly distinguished:
                [0-2233] list
                  [0-2234] listitem
                    [0-4982] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4983] code
                      [0-2235] StaticText: b
                    [0-2236] StaticText: (single lowercase letter)
                  [0-2237] listitem
                    [0-4985] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4986] code
                      [0-2238] StaticText: B
                    [0-2239] StaticText: (single uppercase letter)
                  [0-2240] listitem
                    [0-4988] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4989] code
                      [0-2241] StaticText: lowercase
                  [0-2242] listitem
                    [0-4991] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4992] code
                      [0-2243] StaticText: lower_case_with_underscores
                  [0-2244] listitem
                    [0-4994] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4995] code
                      [0-2245] StaticText: UPPERCASE
                  [0-2246] listitem
                    [0-4997] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4998] code
                      [0-2247] StaticText: UPPER_CASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES
                  [0-2248] listitem
                    [0-5000] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5001] code
                      [0-2249] StaticText: CapitalizedWords
                    [0-2250] StaticText: (or CapWords, or CamelCase – so named because of the bumpy look of its letters
                    [0-2251] link: [4]
                    [0-2253] StaticText: ). This is also sometimes known as StudlyCaps.
                    [0-2254] paragraph
                      [0-2255] StaticText: Note: When using acronyms in CapWords, capitalize all the letters of the acronym. Thus HTTPServerError is better than HttpServerError.
                  [0-2256] listitem
                    [0-5003] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5004] code
                      [0-2257] StaticText: mixedCase
                    [0-2258] StaticText: (differs from CapitalizedWords by initial lowercase character!)
                  [0-2259] listitem
                    [0-5006] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5007] code
                      [0-2260] StaticText: Capitalized_Words_With_Underscores
                    [0-2261] StaticText: (ugly!)
                [0-2262] paragraph
                  [0-2263] StaticText: There’s also the style of using a short unique prefix to group related names together. This is not used much in Python, but it is mentioned for completeness. For example, the
                  [0-5009] code
                    [0-2264] StaticText: os.stat()
                  [0-2265] StaticText: function returns a tuple whose items traditionally have names like
                  [0-5011] code
                    [0-2266] StaticText: st_mode
                  [0-2267] StaticText: ,
                  [0-5013] code
                    [0-2268] StaticText: st_size
                  [0-2269] StaticText: ,
                  [0-5015] code
                    [0-2270] StaticText: st_mtime
                  [0-2271] StaticText: and so on. (This is done to emphasize the correspondence with the fields of the POSIX system call struct, which helps programmers familiar with that.)
                [0-2272] paragraph
                  [0-2273] StaticText: The X11 library uses a leading X for all its public functions. In Python, this style is generally deemed unnecessary because attribute and method names are prefixed with an object, and function names are prefixed with a module name.
                [0-2274] paragraph
                  [0-2275] StaticText: In addition, the following special forms using leading or trailing underscores are recognized (these can generally be combined with any case convention):
                [0-2276] list
                  [0-2277] listitem
                    [0-5017] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5018] code
                      [0-2278] StaticText: _single_leading_underscore
                    [0-2279] StaticText: : weak “internal use” indicator. E.g.
                    [0-5020] code
                      [0-2280] StaticText: from
                      [0-5787] StaticText: 
                      [0-2281] StaticText: M
                      [0-5788] StaticText: 
                      [0-2282] StaticText: import
                      [0-5789] StaticText: 
                      [0-2283] StaticText: *
                    [0-2284] StaticText: does not import objects whose names start with an underscore.
                  [0-2285] listitem
                    [0-5025] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5026] code
                      [0-2286] StaticText: single_trailing_underscore_
                    [0-2287] StaticText: : used by convention to avoid conflicts with Python keyword, e.g. :
                    [0-2288] pre
                      [0-2289] StaticText: tkinter
                      [0-2290] StaticText: .
                      [0-2291] StaticText: Toplevel
                      [0-2292] StaticText: (
                      [0-2293] StaticText: master
                      [0-2294] StaticText: ,
                      [0-2295] StaticText: 
                      [0-2296] StaticText: class_
                      [0-2297] StaticText: =
                      [0-2298] StaticText: 'ClassName'
                      [0-2299] StaticText: )
                      [0-2300] StaticText: 
                  [0-2301] listitem
                    [0-5041] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5042] code
                      [0-2302] StaticText: __double_leading_underscore
                    [0-2303] StaticText: : when naming a class attribute, invokes name mangling (inside class FooBar,
                    [0-5044] code
                      [0-2304] StaticText: __boo
                    [0-2305] StaticText: becomes
                    [0-5046] code
                      [0-2306] StaticText: _FooBar__boo
                    [0-2307] StaticText: ; see below).
                  [0-2308] listitem
                    [0-5048] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5049] code
                      [0-2309] StaticText: __double_leading_and_trailing_underscore__
                    [0-2310] StaticText: : “magic” objects or attributes that live in user-controlled namespaces. E.g.
                    [0-5051] code
                      [0-2311] StaticText: __init__
                    [0-2312] StaticText: ,
                    [0-5053] code
                      [0-2313] StaticText: __import__
                    [0-2314] StaticText: or
                    [0-5055] code
                      [0-2315] StaticText: __file__
                    [0-2316] StaticText: . Never invent such names; only use them as documented.
              [0-2317] section
                [0-2318] heading: Prescriptive: Naming Conventions
                  [0-2319] doc-backlink: Prescriptive: Naming Conventions
                [0-2321] section
                  [0-2322] heading: Names to Avoid
                    [0-2323] doc-backlink: Names to Avoid
                  [0-2325] paragraph
                    [0-2326] StaticText: Never use the characters ‘l’ (lowercase letter el), ‘O’ (uppercase letter oh), or ‘I’ (uppercase letter eye) as single character variable names.
                  [0-2327] paragraph
                    [0-2328] StaticText: In some fonts, these characters are indistinguishable from the numerals one and zero. When tempted to use ‘l’, use ‘L’ instead.
                [0-2329] section
                  [0-2330] heading: ASCII Compatibility
                    [0-2331] doc-backlink: ASCII Compatibility
                  [0-2333] paragraph
                    [0-2334] StaticText: Identifiers used in the standard library must be ASCII compatible as described in the
                    [0-2335] link: policy section
                    [0-2337] StaticText: of
                    [0-2338] link: PEP 3131
                    [0-2340] StaticText: .
                [0-2341] section
                  [0-2342] heading: Package and Module Names
                    [0-2343] doc-backlink: Package and Module Names
                  [0-2345] paragraph
                    [0-2346] StaticText: Modules should have short, all-lowercase names. Underscores can be used in the module name if it improves readability. Python packages should also have short, all-lowercase names, although the use of underscores is discouraged.
                  [0-2347] paragraph
                    [0-2348] StaticText: When an extension module written in C or C++ has an accompanying Python module that provides a higher level (e.g. more object oriented) interface, the C/C++ module has a leading underscore (e.g.
                    [0-5057] code
                      [0-2349] StaticText: _socket
                    [0-2350] StaticText: ).
                [0-2351] section
                  [0-2352] heading: Class Names
                    [0-2353] doc-backlink: Class Names
                  [0-2355] paragraph

                  [0-2439] heading: Function and Variable Names

                  [0-2442] paragraph
                    [0-2443] StaticText: Function names should be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary to improve readability.

                  [0-2446] paragraph

                [0-2448] section
                  [0-2449] heading: Function and Method Arguments

                  [0-2452] paragraph
                    [0-2453] StaticText: Always use

                    [0-2455] StaticText: for the first argument to instance methods.
                  [0-2456] paragraph
                    [0-2457] StaticText: Always use

                    [0-2459] StaticText: for the first argument to class methods.
                  [0-2460] paragraph
                    [0-2461] StaticText: If a function argument’s name clashes with a reserved keyword, it is generally better to append a single trailing underscore rather than use an abbreviation or spelling corruption. Thus
                    [0-5109] code

                    [0-2463] StaticText: is better than

                [0-2466] section
                  [0-2467] heading: Method Names and Instance Variables
                    [0-2468] doc-backlink: Method Names and Instance Variables
                  [0-2470] paragraph
                    [0-2471] StaticText: Use the function naming rules: lowercase with words separated by underscores as necessary to improve readability.
                  [0-2472] paragraph
                    [0-2473] StaticText: Use one leading underscore only for non-public methods and instance variables.
                  [0-2474] paragraph
                    [0-2475] StaticText: To avoid name clashes with subclasses, use two leading underscores to invoke Python’s name mangling rules.
                  [0-2476] paragraph
                    [0-2477] StaticText: Python mangles these names with the class name: if class Foo has an attribute named
                    [0-5113] code
                      [0-2478] StaticText: __a
                    [0-2479] StaticText: , it cannot be accessed by
                    [0-5115] code
                      [0-2480] StaticText: Foo.__a
                    [0-2481] StaticText: . (An insistent user could still gain access by calling
                    [0-5117] code
                      [0-2482] StaticText: Foo._Foo__a
                    [0-2483] StaticText: .) Generally, double leading underscores should be used only to avoid name conflicts with attributes in classes designed to be subclassed.
                  [0-2484] paragraph
                    [0-2485] StaticText: Note: there is some controversy about the use of __names (see below).
                [0-2486] section
                  [0-2487] heading: Constants
                    [0-2488] doc-backlink: Constants
                  [0-2490] paragraph
                    [0-2491] StaticText: Constants are usually defined on a module level and written in all capital letters with underscores separating words. Examples include
                    [0-5119] code

                [0-2496] section
                  [0-2497] heading: Designing for Inheritance
                    [0-2498] doc-backlink: Designing for Inheritance
                  [0-2500] paragraph
                    [0-2501] StaticText: Always decide whether a class’s methods and instance variables (collectively: “attributes”) should be public or non-public. If in doubt, choose non-public; it’s easier to make it public later than to make a public attribute non-public.
                  [0-2502] paragraph
                    [0-2503] StaticText: Public attributes are those that you expect unrelated clients of your class to use, with your commitment to avoid backwards incompatible changes. Non-public attributes are those that are not intended to be used by third parties; you make no guarantees that non-public attributes won’t change or even be removed.
                  [0-2504] paragraph
                    [0-2505] StaticText: We don’t use the term “private” here, since no attribute is really private in Python (without a generally unnecessary amount of work).
                  [0-2506] paragraph
                    [0-2507] StaticText: Another category of attributes are those that are part of the “subclass API” (often called “protected” in other languages). Some classes are designed to be inherited from, either to extend or modify aspects of the class’s behavior. When designing such a class, take care to make explicit decisions about which attributes are public, which are part of the subclass API, and which are truly only to be used by your base class.
                  [0-2508] paragraph
                    [0-2509] StaticText: With this in mind, here are the Pythonic guidelines:
                  [0-2510] list
                    [0-2511] listitem
                      [0-5123] ListMarker: •
                      [0-2512] StaticText: Public attributes should have no leading underscores.
                    [0-2513] listitem
                      [0-5124] ListMarker: •
                      [0-2514] StaticText: If your public attribute name collides with a reserved keyword, append a single trailing underscore to your attribute name. This is preferable to an abbreviation or corrupted spelling. (However, notwithstanding this rule, ‘cls’ is the preferred spelling for any variable or argument which is known to be a class, especially the first argument to a class method.)
                      [0-2515] paragraph
                        [0-2516] StaticText: Note 1: See the argument name recommendation above for class methods.
                    [0-2517] listitem
                      [0-5125] ListMarker: •
                      [0-2518] StaticText: For simple public data attributes, it is best to expose just the attribute name, without complicated accessor/mutator methods. Keep in mind that Python provides an easy path to future enhancement, should you find that a simple data attribute needs to grow functional behavior. In that case, use properties to hide functional implementation behind simple data attribute access syntax.
                      [0-2519] paragraph
                        [0-2520] StaticText: Note 1: Try to keep the functional behavior side-effect free, although side-effects such as caching are generally fine.
                      [0-2521] paragraph
                        [0-2522] StaticText: Note 2: Avoid using properties for computationally expensive operations; the attribute notation makes the caller believe that access is (relatively) cheap.
                    [0-2523] listitem
                      [0-5126] ListMarker: •
                      [0-2524] StaticText: If your class is intended to be subclassed, and you have attributes that you do not want subclasses to use, consider naming them with double leading underscores and no trailing underscores. This invokes Python’s name mangling algorithm, where the name of the class is mangled into the attribute name. This helps avoid attribute name collisions should subclasses inadvertently contain attributes with the same name.
                      [0-2525] paragraph
                        [0-2526] StaticText: Note 1: Note that only the simple class name is used in the mangled name, so if a subclass chooses both the same class name and attribute name, you can still get name collisions.
                      [0-2527] paragraph
                        [0-2528] StaticText: Note 2: Name mangling can make certain uses, such as debugging and
                        [0-5127] code
                          [0-2529] StaticText: __getattr__()
                        [0-2530] StaticText: , less convenient. However the name mangling algorithm is well documented and easy to perform manually.
                      [0-2531] paragraph
                        [0-2532] StaticText: Note 3: Not everyone likes name mangling. Try to balance the need to avoid accidental name clashes with potential use by advanced callers.
              [0-2533] section
                [0-2534] heading: Public and Internal Interfaces
                  [0-2535] doc-backlink: Public and Internal Interfaces
                [0-2537] paragraph
                  [0-2538] StaticText: Any backwards compatibility guarantees apply only to public interfaces. Accordingly, it is important that users be able to clearly distinguish between public and internal interfaces.
                [0-2539] paragraph
                  [0-2540] StaticText: Documented interfaces are considered public, unless the documentation explicitly declares them to be provisional or internal interfaces exempt from the usual backwards compatibility guarantees. All undocumented interfaces should be assumed to be internal.
                [0-2541] paragraph
                  [0-2542] StaticText: To better support introspection, modules should explicitly declare the names in their public API using the
                  [0-5129] code

                  [0-2544] StaticText: attribute. Setting
                  [0-5131] code
                    [0-2545] StaticText: __all__
                  [0-2546] StaticText: to an empty list indicates that the module has no public API.
                [0-2547] paragraph
                  [0-2548] StaticText: Even with
                  [0-5133] code
                    [0-2549] StaticText: __all__
                  [0-2550] StaticText: set appropriately, internal interfaces (packages, modules, classes, functions, attributes or other names) should still be prefixed with a single leading underscore.
                [0-2551] paragraph
                  [0-2552] StaticText: An interface is also considered internal if any containing namespace (package, module or class) is considered internal.
                [0-2553] paragraph
                  [0-2554] StaticText: Imported names should always be considered an implementation detail. Other modules must not rely on indirect access to such imported names unless they are an explicitly documented part of the containing module’s API, such as
                  [0-5135] code

                  [0-5137] code

                    [0-2745] StaticText: Class naming conventions apply here, although you should add the suffix “Error” to your exception classes if the exception is an error. Non-error exceptions that are used for non-local flow control or other forms of signaling need no special suffix.

                    [0-2794] StaticText: A good rule of thumb is to limit use of bare ‘except’ clauses to two cases:

                [0-3222] heading: Function Annotations
                  [0-3223] doc-backlink: Function Annotations
                [0-3225] paragraph
                  [0-3226] StaticText: With the acceptance of
                  [0-3227] link: PEP 484
                  [0-3229] StaticText: , the style rules for function annotations have changed.
                [0-3230] list
                  [0-3231] listitem
                    [0-5637] ListMarker: •
                    [0-3232] StaticText: Function annotations should use
                    [0-3233] link: PEP 484
                    [0-3235] StaticText: syntax (there are some formatting recommendations for annotations in the previous section).
                  [0-3236] listitem
                    [0-5638] ListMarker: •
                    [0-3237] StaticText: The experimentation with annotation styles that was recommended previously in this PEP is no longer encouraged.
                  [0-3238] listitem
                    [0-5639] ListMarker: •
                    [0-3239] StaticText: However, outside the stdlib, experiments within the rules of
                    [0-3240] link: PEP 484
                    [0-3242] StaticText: are now encouraged. For example, marking up a large third party library or application with
                    [0-3243] link: PEP 484
                    [0-3245] StaticText: style type annotations, reviewing how easy it was to add those annotations, and observing whether their presence increases code understandability.
                  [0-3246] listitem
                    [0-5640] ListMarker: •
                    [0-3247] StaticText: The Python standard library should be conservative in adopting such annotations, but their use is allowed for new code and for big refactorings.
                  [0-3248] listitem
                    [0-5641] ListMarker: •
                    [0-3249] StaticText: For code that wants to make a different use of function annotations it is recommended to put a comment of the form:
                    [0-3250] pre
                      [0-3251] StaticText: # type: ignore
                      [0-3252] StaticText: 
                    [0-3253] paragraph
                      [0-3254] StaticText: near the top of the file; this tells type checkers to ignore all annotations. (More fine-grained ways of disabling complaints from type checkers can be found in
                      [0-3255] link: PEP 484
                      [0-3257] StaticText: .)
                  [0-3258] listitem
                    [0-5646] ListMarker: •
                    [0-3259] StaticText: Like linters, type checkers are optional, separate tools. Python interpreters by default should not issue any messages due to type checking and should not alter their behavior based on annotations.
                  [0-3260] listitem
                    [0-5647] ListMarker: •
                    [0-3261] StaticText: Users who don’t want to use type checkers are free to ignore them. However, it is expected that users of third party library packages may want to run type checkers over those packages. For this purpose
                    [0-3262] link: PEP 484
                    [0-3264] StaticText: recommends the use of stub files: .pyi files that are read by the type checker in preference of the corresponding .py files. Stub files can be distributed with a library, or separately (with the library author’s permission) through the typeshed repo
                    [0-3265] link: [5]
                    [0-3267] StaticText: .

              [0-53] paragraph
                [0-247] StaticText: This document gives coding conventions for the Python code comprising the standard library in the main Python distribution. Please see the companion informational PEP describing
                [0-248] link: style guidelines for the C code in the C implementation of Python

              [0-251] paragraph
                [0-252] StaticText: This document and
                [0-253] link: PEP 257
                [0-255] StaticText: (Docstring Conventions) were adapted from Guido’s original Python Style Guide essay, with some additions from Barry’s style guide
                [0-256] link: [2]
                [0-258] StaticText: .
              [0-259] paragraph
                [0-260] StaticText: This style guide evolves over time as additional conventions are identified and past conventions are rendered obsolete by changes in the language itself.
              [0-261] paragraph
                [0-262] StaticText: Many projects have their own coding style guidelines. In the event of any conflicts, such project-specific guides take precedence for that project.
            [0-263] section
              [0-264] heading: A Foolish Consistency is the Hobgoblin of Little Minds
                [0-265] doc-backlink: A Foolish Consistency is the Hobgoblin of Little Minds
              [0-267] paragraph
                [0-268] StaticText: One of Guido’s key insights is that code is read much more often than it is written. The guidelines provided here are intended to improve the readability of code and make it consistent across the wide spectrum of Python code. As
                [0-269] link: PEP 20
                [0-271] StaticText: says, “Readability counts”.
              [0-54] paragraph
                [0-272] StaticText: A style guide is about consistency. Consistency with this style guide is important. Consistency within a project is more important. Consistency within one module or function is the most important.
              [0-273] paragraph
                [0-274] StaticText: However, know when to be inconsistent – sometimes style guide recommendations just aren’t applicable. When in doubt, use your best judgment. Look at other examples and decide what looks best. And don’t hesitate to ask!
              [0-275] paragraph
                [0-276] StaticText: In particular: do not break backwards compatibility just to comply with this PEP!
              [0-277] paragraph
                [0-278] StaticText: Some other good reasons to ignore a particular guideline:
              [0-279] list
                [0-280] listitem
                  [0-3736] ListMarker: 1.
                  [0-281] StaticText: When applying the guideline would make the code less readable, even for someone who is used to reading code that follows this PEP.
                [0-282] listitem
                  [0-3737] ListMarker: 2.
                  [0-283] StaticText: To be consistent with surrounding code that also breaks it (maybe for historic reasons) – although this is also an opportunity to clean up someone else’s mess (in true XP style).
                [0-284] listitem
                  [0-3738] ListMarker: 3.
                  [0-285] StaticText: Because the code in question predates the introduction of the guideline and there is no other reason to be modifying that code.
                [0-286] listitem
                  [0-3739] ListMarker: 4.
                  [0-287] StaticText: When the code needs to remain compatible with older versions of Python that don’t support the feature recommended by the style guide.

              [0-619] section
                [0-620] heading: Tabs or Spaces?
                  [0-621] doc-backlink: Tabs or Spaces?
                [0-623] paragraph
                  [0-624] StaticText: Spaces are the preferred indentation method.
                [0-625] paragraph
                  [0-626] StaticText: Tabs should be used solely to remain consistent with code that is already indented with tabs.
                [0-627] paragraph
                  [0-628] StaticText: Python disallows mixing tabs and spaces for indentation.
              [0-629] section
                [0-630] heading: Maximum Line Length
                  [0-631] doc-backlink: Maximum Line Length
                [0-633] paragraph
                  [0-634] StaticText: Limit all lines to a maximum of 79 characters.
                [0-635] paragraph
                  [0-636] StaticText: For flowing long blocks of text with fewer structural restrictions (docstrings or comments), the line length should be limited to 72 characters.
                [0-637] paragraph
                  [0-638] StaticText: Limiting the required editor window width makes it possible to have several files open side by side, and works well when using code review tools that present the two versions in adjacent columns.
                [0-639] paragraph
                  [0-640] StaticText: The default wrapping in most tools disrupts the visual structure of the code, making it more difficult to understand. The limits are chosen to avoid wrapping in editors with the window width set to 80, even if the tool places a marker glyph in the final column when wrapping lines. Some web based tools may not offer dynamic line wrapping at all.
                [0-641] paragraph
                  [0-642] StaticText: Some teams strongly prefer a longer line length. For code maintained exclusively or primarily by a team that can reach agreement on this issue, it is okay to increase the line length limit up to 99 characters, provided that comments and docstrings are still wrapped at 72 characters.
                [0-643] paragraph
                  [0-644] StaticText: The Python standard library is conservative and requires limiting lines to 79 characters (and docstrings/comments to 72).
                [0-645] paragraph
                  [0-646] StaticText: The preferred way of wrapping long lines is by using Python’s implied line continuation inside parentheses, brackets and braces. Long lines can be broken over multiple lines by wrapping expressions in parentheses. These should be used in preference to using a backslash for line continuation.
                [0-647] paragraph
                  [0-648] StaticText: Backslashes may still be appropriate at times. For example, long, multiple
                  [0-3950] code

                  [0-650] StaticText: -statements could not use implicit continuation before Python 3.10, so backslashes were acceptable for that case:

                [0-700] heading: Should a Line Break Before or After a Binary Operator?
                  [0-701] doc-backlink: Should a Line Break Before or After a Binary Operator?
                [0-703] paragraph
                  [0-704] StaticText: For decades the recommended style was to break after binary operators. But this can hurt readability in two ways: the operators tend to get scattered across different columns on the screen, and each operator is moved away from its operand and onto the previous line. Here, the eye has to do extra work to tell which items are added and which are subtracted:

                  [0-707] StaticText: 
                  [0-708] StaticText: # operators sit far away from their operands

                  [0-741] StaticText: To solve this readability problem, mathematicians and their publishers follow the opposite convention. Donald Knuth explains the traditional rule in his

              [0-786] section
                [0-787] heading: Blank Lines
                  [0-788] doc-backlink: Blank Lines
                [0-790] paragraph
                  [0-791] StaticText: Surround top-level function and class definitions with two blank lines.
                [0-792] paragraph
                  [0-793] StaticText: Method definitions inside a class are surrounded by a single blank line.
                [0-794] paragraph
                  [0-795] StaticText: Extra blank lines may be used (sparingly) to separate groups of related functions. Blank lines may be omitted between a bunch of related one-liners (e.g. a set of dummy implementations).
                [0-796] paragraph
                  [0-797] StaticText: Use blank lines in functions, sparingly, to indicate logical sections.
                [0-798] paragraph
                  [0-799] StaticText: Python accepts the control-L (i.e. ^L) form feed character as whitespace; many tools treat these characters as page separators, so you may use them to separate pages of related sections of your file. Note, some editors and web-based code viewers may not recognize control-L as a form feed and will show another glyph in its place.
              [0-800] section
                [0-801] heading: Source File Encoding
                  [0-802] doc-backlink: Source File Encoding
                [0-804] paragraph
                  [0-805] StaticText: Code in the core Python distribution should always use UTF-8, and should not have an encoding declaration.
                [0-806] paragraph
                  [0-807] StaticText: In the standard library, non-UTF-8 encodings should be used only for test purposes. Use non-ASCII characters sparingly, preferably only to denote places and human names. If using non-ASCII characters as data, avoid noisy Unicode characters like z̯̯͡a̧͎̺l̡͓̫g̹̲o̡̼̘ and byte order marks.
                [0-808] paragraph
                  [0-809] StaticText: All identifiers in the Python standard library MUST use ASCII-only identifiers, and SHOULD use English words wherever feasible (in many cases, abbreviations and technical terms are used which aren’t English).
                [0-810] paragraph
                  [0-811] StaticText: Open source projects with a global audience are encouraged to adopt a similar policy.

                    [0-857] StaticText: Imports are always put at the top of the file, just after any module comments and docstrings, and before module globals and constants.

                    [0-867] paragraph
                      [0-868] StaticText: You should put a blank line between each group of imports.
                  [0-869] listitem
                    [0-4067] ListMarker: •
                    [0-870] StaticText: Absolute imports are recommended, as they are usually more readable and tend to be better behaved (or at least give better error messages) if the import system is incorrectly configured (such as when a directory inside a package ends up on

              [0-1026] heading: String Quotes
                [0-1027] doc-backlink: String Quotes
              [0-1029] paragraph
                [0-1030] StaticText: In Python, single-quoted strings and double-quoted strings are the same. This PEP does not make a recommendation for this. Pick a rule and stick to it. When a string contains single or double quote characters, however, use the other one to avoid backslashes in the string. It improves readability.
              [0-1031] paragraph
                [0-1032] StaticText: For triple-quoted strings, always use double quote characters to be consistent with the docstring convention in
                [0-1033] link: PEP 257

                    [0-1470] StaticText: Avoid trailing whitespace anywhere.             [0-2032] section
              [0-2033] heading: When to Use Trailing Commas
                [0-2034] doc-backlink: When to Use Trailing Commas
              [0-2036] paragraph
                [0-2037] StaticText: Trailing commas are usually optional, except they are mandatory when making a tuple of one element. For clarity, it is recommended to surround the latter in (technically redundant) parentheses:
              [0-2038] pre
                [0-2039] StaticText: # Correct:
                [0-2040] StaticText: 
                [0-2041] StaticText: FILES
                [0-2042] StaticText: 
                [0-2043] StaticText: =
                [0-2044] StaticText: 
                [0-2045] StaticText: (
                [0-2046] StaticText: 'setup.cfg'
                [0-2047] StaticText: ,)
                [0-2048] StaticText: 
              [0-2049] pre
                [0-2050] StaticText: # Wrong:
                [0-2051] StaticText: 
                [0-2052] StaticText: FILES
                [0-2053] StaticText: 
                [0-2054] StaticText: =
                [0-2055] StaticText: 
                [0-2056] StaticText: 'setup.cfg'
                [0-2057] StaticText: ,
                [0-2058] StaticText: 
              [0-2059] paragraph
                [0-2060] StaticText: When trailing commas are redundant, they are often helpful when a version control system is used, when a list of values, arguments or imported items is expected to be extended over time. The pattern is to put each value (etc.) on a line by itself, always adding a trailing comma, and add the close parenthesis/bracket/brace on the next line. However it does not make sense to have a trailing comma on the same line as the closing delimiter (except in the above case of singleton tuples):
              [0-2061] pre
                [0-2062] StaticText: # Correct:
                [0-2063] StaticText:

            [0-2114] section
              [0-2115] heading: Comments
                [0-48] doc-backlink: Comments
              [0-2117] paragraph
                [0-2118] StaticText: Comments that contradict the code are worse than no comments. Always make a priority of keeping the comments up-to-date when the code changes!
              [0-2119] paragraph
                [0-2120] StaticText: Comments should be complete sentences. The first word should be capitalized, unless it is an identifier that begins with a lower case letter (never alter the case of identifiers!).
              [0-2121] paragraph
                [0-2122] StaticText: Block comments generally consist of one or more paragraphs built out of complete sentences, with each sentence ending in a period.
              [0-2123] paragraph
                [0-2124] StaticText: You should use one or two spaces after a sentence-ending period in multi-sentence comments, except after the final sentence.
              [0-2125] paragraph
                [0-2126] StaticText: Ensure that your comments are clear and easily understandable to other speakers of the language you are writing in.
              [0-2127] paragraph
                [0-2128] StaticText: Python coders from non-English speaking countries: please write your comments in English, unless you are 120% sure that the code will never be read by people who don’t speak your language.
              [0-2129] section
                [0-2130] heading: Block Comments
                  [0-2131] doc-backlink: Block Comments
                [0-2133] paragraph
                  [0-2134] StaticText: Block comments generally apply to some (or all) code that follows them, and are indented to the same level as that code. Each line of a block comment starts with a
                  [0-4941] code
                    [0-2135] StaticText: #
                  [0-2136] StaticText: and a single space (unless it is indented text inside the comment).
                [0-2137] paragraph
                  [0-2138] StaticText: Paragraphs inside a block comment are separated by a line containing a single
                  [0-4943] code
                    [0-2139] StaticText: #
                  [0-2140] StaticText: .
              [0-2141] section
                [0-2142] heading: Inline Comments
                  [0-2143] doc-backlink: Inline Comments
                [0-2145] paragraph
                  [0-2146] StaticText: Use inline comments sparingly.
                [0-2147] paragraph
                  [0-2148] StaticText: An inline comment is a comment on the same line as a statement. Inline comments should be separated by at least two spaces from the statement. They should start with a # and a single space.
                [0-2149] paragraph
                  [0-2150] StaticText: Inline comments are unnecessary and in fact distracting if they state the obvious. Don’t do this:

                  [0-2181] doc-backlink: Documentation Strings
                [0-2183] paragraph
                  [0-2184] StaticText: Conventions for writing good documentation strings (a.k.a. “docstrings”) are immortalized in
                  [0-2185] link: PEP 257
                  [0-2187] StaticText: .
                [0-2188] list
                  [0-2189] listitem
                    [0-4963] ListMarker: •
                    [0-2190] StaticText: Write docstrings for all public modules, functions, classes, and methods. Docstrings are not necessary for non-public methods, but you should have a comment that describes what the method does. This comment should appear after the
                    [0-4964] code
                      [0-2191] StaticText: def
                    [0-2192] StaticText: line.

                    [0-2196] StaticText: describes good docstring conventions. Note that most importantly, the
                    [0-4967] code

                    [0-4976] code

            [0-2213] section
              [0-2214] heading: Naming Conventions
                [0-2215] doc-backlink: Naming Conventions
              [0-2217] paragraph
                [0-2218] StaticText: The naming conventions of Python’s library are a bit of a mess, so we’ll never get this completely consistent – nevertheless, here are the currently recommended naming standards. New modules and packages (including third party frameworks) should be written to these standards, but where an existing library has a different style, internal consistency is preferred.
              [0-2219] section
                [0-2220] heading: Overriding Principle
                  [0-2221] doc-backlink: Overriding Principle
                [0-2223] paragraph
                  [0-2224] StaticText: Names that are visible to the user as public parts of the API should follow conventions that reflect usage rather than implementation.
              [0-2225] section
                [0-2226] heading: Descriptive: Naming Styles
                  [0-2227] doc-backlink: Descriptive: Naming Styles
                [0-2229] paragraph
                  [0-2230] StaticText: There are a lot of different naming styles. It helps to be able to recognize what naming style is being used, independently from what they are used for.
                [0-2231] paragraph
                  [0-2232] StaticText: The following naming styles are commonly distinguished:
                [0-2233] list
                  [0-2234] listitem
                    [0-4982] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4983] code
                      [0-2235] StaticText: b
                    [0-2236] StaticText: (single lowercase letter)
                  [0-2237] listitem
                    [0-4985] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4986] code
                      [0-2238] StaticText: B
                    [0-2239] StaticText: (single uppercase letter)
                  [0-2240] listitem
                    [0-4988] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4989] code
                      [0-2241] StaticText: lowercase
                  [0-2242] listitem
                    [0-4991] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4992] code
                      [0-2243] StaticText: lower_case_with_underscores
                  [0-2244] listitem
                    [0-4994] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4995] code
                      [0-2245] StaticText: UPPERCASE
                  [0-2246] listitem
                    [0-4997] ListMarker: •
                    [0-4998] code
                      [0-2247] StaticText: UPPER_CASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES
                  [0-2248] listitem
                    [0-5000] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5001] code
                      [0-2249] StaticText: CapitalizedWords
                    [0-2250] StaticText: (or CapWords, or CamelCase – so named because of the bumpy look of its letters
                    [0-2251] link: [4]
                    [0-2253] StaticText: ). This is also sometimes known as StudlyCaps.
                    [0-2254] paragraph
                      [0-2255] StaticText: Note: When using acronyms in CapWords, capitalize all the letters of the acronym. Thus HTTPServerError is better than HttpServerError.
                  [0-2256] listitem
                    [0-5003] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5004] code
                      [0-2257] StaticText: mixedCase
                    [0-2258] StaticText: (differs from CapitalizedWords by initial lowercase character!)
                  [0-2259] listitem
                    [0-5006] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5007] code
                      [0-2260] StaticText: Capitalized_Words_With_Underscores
                    [0-2261] StaticText: (ugly!)
                [0-2262] paragraph
                  [0-2263] StaticText: There’s also the style of using a short unique prefix to group related names together. This is not used much in Python, but it is mentioned for completeness. For example, the
                  [0-5009] code
                    [0-2264] StaticText: os.stat()
                  [0-2265] StaticText: function returns a tuple whose items traditionally have names like
                  [0-5011] code
                    [0-2266] StaticText: st_mode
                  [0-2267] StaticText: ,
                  [0-5013] code
                    [0-2268] StaticText: st_size
                  [0-2269] StaticText: ,
                  [0-5015] code
                    [0-2270] StaticText: st_mtime
                  [0-2271] StaticText: and so on. (This is done to emphasize the correspondence with the fields of the POSIX system call struct, which helps programmers familiar with that.)
                [0-2272] paragraph
                  [0-2273] StaticText: The X11 library uses a leading X for all its public functions. In Python, this style is generally deemed unnecessary because attribute and method names are prefixed with an object, and function names are prefixed with a module name.
                [0-2274] paragraph
                  [0-2275] StaticText: In addition, the following special forms using leading or trailing underscores are recognized (these can generally be combined with any case convention):
                [0-2276] list
                  [0-2277] listitem
                    [0-5017] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5018] code
                      [0-2278] StaticText: _single_leading_underscore
                    [0-2279] StaticText: : weak “internal use” indicator. E.g.
                    [0-5020] code
                      [0-2280] StaticText: from
                      [0-5787] StaticText: 
                      [0-2281] StaticText: M
                      [0-5788] StaticText: 
                      [0-2282] StaticText: import
                      [0-5789] StaticText: 
                      [0-2283] StaticText: *
                    [0-2284] StaticText: does not import objects whose names start with an underscore.
                  [0-2285] listitem
                    [0-5025] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5026] code
                      [0-2286] StaticText: single_trailing_underscore_
                    [0-2287] StaticText: : used by convention to avoid conflicts with Python keyword, e.g. :
                    [0-2288] pre
                      [0-2289] StaticText: tkinter
                      [0-2290] StaticText: .
                      [0-2291] StaticText: Toplevel
                      [0-2292] StaticText: (
                      [0-2293] StaticText: master
                      [0-2294] StaticText: ,
                      [0-2295] StaticText: 
                      [0-2296] StaticText: class_
                      [0-2297] StaticText: =
                      [0-2298] StaticText: 'ClassName'
                      [0-2299] StaticText: )
                      [0-2300] StaticText: 
                  [0-2301] listitem
                    [0-5041] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5042] code
                      [0-2302] StaticText: __double_leading_underscore
                    [0-2303] StaticText: : when naming a class attribute, invokes name mangling (inside class FooBar,
                    [0-5044] code
                      [0-2304] StaticText: __boo
                    [0-2305] StaticText: becomes
                    [0-5046] code
                      [0-2306] StaticText: _FooBar__boo
                    [0-2307] StaticText: ; see below).
                  [0-2308] listitem
                    [0-5048] ListMarker: •
                    [0-5049] code
                      [0-2309] StaticText: __double_leading_and_trailing_underscore__
                    [0-2310] StaticText: : “magic” objects or attributes that live in user-controlled namespaces. E.g.
                    [0-5051] code
                      [0-2311] StaticText: __init__
                    [0-2312] StaticText: ,
                    [0-5053] code
                      [0-2313] StaticText: __import__
                    [0-2314] StaticText: or
                    [0-5055] code
                      [0-2315] StaticText: __file__
                    [0-2316] StaticText: . Never invent such names; only use them as documented.
              [0-2317] section
                [0-2318] heading: Prescriptive: Naming Conventions
                  [0-2319] doc-backlink: Prescriptive: Naming Conventions
                [0-2321] section
                  [0-2322] heading: Names to Avoid
                    [0-2323] doc-backlink: Names to Avoid
                  [0-2325] paragraph
                    [0-2326] StaticText: Never use the characters ‘l’ (lowercase letter el), ‘O’ (uppercase letter oh), or ‘I’ (uppercase letter eye) as single character variable names.
                  [0-2327] paragraph
                    [0-2328] StaticText: In some fonts, these characters are indistinguishable from the numerals one and zero. When tempted to use ‘l’, use ‘L’ instead.
                [0-2329] section
                  [0-2330] heading: ASCII Compatibility
                    [0-2331] doc-backlink: ASCII Compatibility
                  [0-2333] paragraph
                    [0-2334] StaticText: Identifiers used in the standard library must be ASCII compatible as described in the
                    [0-2335] link: policy section
                    [0-2337] StaticText: of
                    [0-2338] link: PEP 3131
                    [0-2340] StaticText: .
                [0-2341] section
                  [0-2342] heading: Package and Module Names
                    [0-2343] doc-backlink: Package and Module Names
                  [0-2345] paragraph
                    [0-2346] StaticText: Modules should have short, all-lowercase names. Underscores can be used in the module name if it improves readability. Python packages should also have short, all-lowercase names, although the use of underscores is discouraged.
                  [0-2347] paragraph
                    [0-2348] StaticText: When an extension module written in C or C++ has an accompanying Python module that provides a higher level (e.g. more object oriented) interface, the C/C++ module has a leading underscore (e.g.
                    [0-5057] code
                      [0-2349] StaticText: _socket
                    [0-2350] StaticText: ).
                [0-2351] section
                  [0-2352] heading: Class Names
                    [0-2353] doc-backlink: Class Names
                  [0-2355] paragraph
                    [0-2356] StaticText: Class names should normally use the CapWords convention.
                  [0-2357] paragraph
                    [0-2358] StaticText: The naming convention for functions may be used instead in cases where the interface is documented and used primarily as a callable.
                  [0-2359] paragraph
                    [0-2360] StaticText: Note that there is a separate convention for builtin names: most builtin names are single words (or two words run together), with the CapWords convention used only for exception names and builtin constants.
                [0-2361] section
                  [0-2362] heading: Type Variable Names
                    [0-2363] doc-backlink: Type Variable Names
                  [0-2365] paragraph
                    [0-2366] StaticText: Names of type variables introduced in
                    [0-2367] link: PEP 484
                    [0-2369] StaticText: should normally use CapWords preferring short names:
                    [0-5059] code
                      [0-2370] StaticText: T
                    [0-2371] StaticText: ,
                    [0-5061] code
                      [0-2372] StaticText: AnyStr
                    [0-2373] StaticText: ,
                    [0-5063] code
                      [0-2374] StaticText: Num
                    [0-2375] StaticText: . It is recommended to add suffixes
                    [0-5065] code
                      [0-2376] StaticText: _co
                    [0-2377] StaticText: or
                    [0-5067] code
                      [0-2378] StaticText: _contra
                    [0-2379] StaticText: to the variables used to declare covariant or contravariant behavior correspondingly:
                  [0-2380] pre
                    [0-2381] StaticText: from
                    [0-2382] StaticText: 
                    [0-2383] StaticText: typing
                    [0-2384] StaticText: 
                    [0-2385] StaticText: import
                    [0-2386] StaticText: 
                    [0-2387] StaticText: TypeVar
                    [0-2388] StaticText: 
                    [0-2389] StaticText: VT_co
                    [0-2390] StaticText: 
                    [0-2391] StaticText: =
                    [0-2392] StaticText: 
                    [0-2393] StaticText: TypeVar
                    [0-2394] StaticText: (

                    [0-2397] StaticText:
